title: Tariffs: Who Really Pays (the Receipts)
note: EP026 — explainer (By the Numbers, row 15). Tariffs are paid by the importer and passed to consumers; the trade-war receipts. Free memes; 4 new motifs (passthrough, tradewar, customsgate, deadweight). Target 12–15 min.

scenes.narration: Here's a sentence you've heard a hundred times from politicians of every stripe. 'We'll put tariffs on China, and China will pay.' It sounds tough, and it sounds free. It's also, mostly, false.
Because a tariff is a tax. And the uncomfortable truth, written in black and white on the receipts, is that the people who overwhelmingly pay it are… you.
The politician says a foreign country is footing the bill. Your shopping cart quietly disagrees.
scenes.memeBottom: you pay it at the checkout

scenes.narration: Economists studied the 2018 and 2019 trade war in detail, and the verdict was blunt: the cost landed almost entirely on American businesses and consumers.

Take a real example: washing machines. After tariffs hit them, their prices jumped sharply — and here's the kicker, dryers got more expensive too, even though dryers weren't tariffed. The makers simply raised both.
So how does a tax that's supposed to punish foreigners end up in your receipts? Let's follow the money, step by step — and read the actual receipts.
So let's settle it for good — who actually pays a tariff, and who really wins and loses.
scenes.heading: Tariffs: Who Really Pays
scenes.sub: A tax on foreigners — paid by you.

scenes.narration: The gap between the slogan and the checkout is the whole story.
Start with what a tariff actually is. It's a tax on imported goods.
And importing just means buying goods made in another country and bringing them home to sell.
Here's the detail everything hinges on. The tariff is not paid by the foreign factory. It's paid by the importer — a domestic company — at the moment the goods cross the border.
Picture the border as a tollbooth. A shipment of goods rolls up — and before it can enter, the American company importing it has to hand the government a cut.
scenes.caption: a tax, stamped on at the border

scenes.narration: The Chinese factory already got paid, in full, for the goods. The check to the US Treasury is written by the American importer. Not Beijing. A company in Ohio.
So right away, 'China pays' is wrong at the most basic, mechanical level. The first check is written by an American. The only question left is what happens next.
Picture a small US business importing phone cases. The tariff bill lands on them, in dollars, due immediately. They either eat it and shrink, or raise prices. Guess which one keeps the lights on.
Trace the whole chain and there's no foreign link in it. Every hand that touches the money, from the border to the till, is domestic.
scenes.caption: no foreign link in the chain

scenes.narration: What happens next is the whole ballgame. It's called pass-through.
scenes.heading: The Pass-Through

scenes.narration: That importer in Ohio isn't a charity. It just paid a new tax on its goods. So it does the obvious thing: it raises its prices to cover the cost.
The tariff gets added at the border, then passed down the chain — from the importer, to the retailer, to the shelf, to the price you pay at the till.
scenes.caption: the tariff rolls downhill to you

scenes.narration: And you can see it in the numbers everyone tracks — the consumer price index, the official measure of what households actually pay.
In the recent trade war, study after study found something striking. Nearly the entire cost of the tariffs showed up in higher US import prices. The pass-through was almost total.
Economists estimated the tariffs cost the typical American household hundreds of dollars a year — a quiet tax increase nobody voted for.
And tariffs are regressive — they hit the poor hardest. A tax on cheap clothes, shoes and electronics takes a far bigger bite out of a tight budget than a comfortable one.
There is simply no way to tax imports without taxing the people who buy them.
The 'tax on China' turned out to be a sales tax on Americans, collected one checkout at a time.
scenes.memeBottom: a tariff is a tax on your own shoppers

scenes.narration: Now, sometimes a foreign exporter does cut its price a little to keep customers — so it eats a sliver. But in the big recent cases, that sliver was tiny. The buyer bore the burden.
But wait — there's a second, sneakier way tariffs raise your prices. And it has nothing to do with imports at all.
scenes.heading: The Hidden Price Hike

scenes.narration: Say a tariff makes foreign steel more expensive. What does the domestic steelmaker — the one you were trying to protect — do next?
scenes.bubble: what does the local firm do?

scenes.narration: It raises its prices too. Why wouldn't it? Its foreign competitor just got more expensive, so it has room to charge more — and pocket the difference.
So you pay more on the imports because of the tax — and more on the domestic versions, because the competition just got softer. You lose on both.
scenes.caption: imported AND domestic prices rise

scenes.narration: This is the real face of protectionism — shielding domestic producers from competition, by making everyone else's option more expensive.
Researchers measured it precisely: when washer tariffs hit, domestic washer prices rose roughly twelve percent too. The protection became a price hike on everyone.
scenes.sub: on domestic washers, after the tariff

scenes.narration: So if consumers lose, who exactly wins? Because tariffs do create winners — just not the ones on the poster.
scenes.heading: Winners and Losers

scenes.narration: Winner one: the protected industry. The specific domestic companies shielded from competition can sell more, and charge more. They love tariffs, and they lobby hard for them.
Winner two: the government, which collects the tariff revenue. Though remember — it's collecting that revenue from its own importers and shoppers.
Now the losers. Loser one, obviously, is you — the consumer paying higher prices on a huge range of everyday goods.
Loser two is sneakier, and often bigger: the domestic manufacturers who use those imported goods as inputs.
Tariff the steel, and you help a few steelmakers — but you hurt every carmaker, appliance maker, and builder who needs steel. And they employ far more people.
The ratio is stark. For every worker in a protected industry like steel, there can be dozens in the industries that USE steel — all now paying more to shield the few.
Economists can even draw the pure waste on a chart — a wedge of value that simply disappears, helping no one. They call it deadweight loss.
scenes.caption: value that just vanishes

scenes.narration: A tariff doesn't just move money from you to a protected company. A chunk of it is destroyed outright — deals that no longer happen, value that's just gone.
There's a brutal arithmetic here. Studies found some tariffs did 'save' jobs — at a cost to consumers of hundreds of thousands, sometimes millions, of dollars per single job saved.
And because the downstream industries got squeezed, the same tariffs often destroyed more jobs than they protected. The visible win quietly hid a larger, invisible loss.
And then there's the part that turns a tax into a war.
scenes.heading: The Trade War

scenes.narration: When one country slaps tariffs on another, the other country rarely just takes it. It retaliates — with tariffs of its own.
That tit-for-tat escalation has a name: a trade war, where countries pile trade barriers on each other.
Now both sides are taxing each other's goods. Both sets of consumers pay more. And exporters on both sides suddenly can't sell abroad.
scenes.caption: tit-for-tat — everyone loses

scenes.narration: And the retaliation always finds your exporters — the farmers, the manufacturers who sell abroad. A tariff thrown outward comes straight back at your own side.
scenes.caption: retaliation hits your exporters

scenes.narration: In the recent US-China war, China retaliated by taxing American farm goods. Suddenly US farmers couldn't sell their soybeans — and their incomes collapsed.
So the government then spent tens of billions bailing out those farmers — using tariff revenue, and more. Taxpayers paid to clean up the mess the tariffs made.
Read that loop again. You paid higher prices at the store. Then your taxes bailed out the exporters hurt by the retaliation. You paid twice.
It's a near-perfect illusion: the cost is real, but it's scattered so thinly across so many receipts that no one feels robbed.
scenes.memeBottom: blaming foreigners while paying the tab

scenes.narration: So the bill actually arrives in three places at once. Higher prices on the shelf. Higher taxes to fund the bailouts. And fewer jobs wherever tariffs raised costs. Three hits, one policy.
There's one more cost that's slower, but maybe the most damaging of all.
scenes.heading: Breaking the Chain

scenes.narration: Modern products aren't made in one country. They're built along a global supply chain, crossing borders many times before they're finished.
A single phone or car might cross borders dozens of times as it's assembled. Tariff each crossing, and the cost stacks up again and again inside one product.
So tariffs don't just tax 'foreign stuff.' They tax the inputs of things made at home — gumming up the whole machine that modern manufacturing depends on.
scenes.caption: taxed at every border crossing

scenes.narration: And the uncertainty alone does damage. If tariffs might appear or vanish at any moment, businesses freeze — afraid to invest, hire, or plan. The chaos itself has a cost.
And timing matters enormously. Pile tariffs onto an economy already fighting inflation, and you're pouring fuel on the fire — pushing the very prices you're trying to tame even higher.
In that situation, a broad tariff is a self-inflicted price rise, hitting at the worst possible moment.
scenes.caption: a self-inflicted price rise

scenes.narration: Now — to be fair, because this isn't quite as simple as 'tariffs always bad.'
scenes.heading: When Tariffs Make Sense

scenes.narration: The opposite of a tariff is free trade — letting goods flow across borders without barriers. It's cheaper, but it isn't costless.
Free trade makes everything cheaper, but it can also hollow out local industries and towns when production moves abroad. Those lost jobs are real.
Which is why economists almost universally prefer helping displaced workers directly — retraining, support, investment — over tariffs that quietly tax everyone to shield a few.
So there are genuine reasons for some tariffs. Protecting a brand-new industry until it can stand on its own. Shielding something vital for national security, like chips or medicine.
Or hitting back when another country cheats — dumping goods below cost to wipe out your producers. Used narrowly and strategically, a tariff can be a real tool.
The honest debate isn't 'free money from foreigners' versus nothing. It's 'cheaper goods' versus 'protected jobs' — and who pays for which.
But that's a trade-off — cheaper goods for all, versus protected jobs for some, paid for by everyone. It is never the free lunch the slogan promises.
The smart version is surgical: narrow tariffs on genuinely strategic goods, paired with real help for the workers and towns that trade leaves behind. Targeted beats blanket, every time.
The clumsy version is a broad tariff on everything — which is really just a giant, hidden national sales tax that happens to sound tough on the campaign trail.
So let's read the final receipt.
scenes.heading: The Final Receipt

scenes.narration: A tariff is a tax on imports. It's paid by the importer. It's passed on to you. And it quietly lets domestic firms raise their prices too.
lines: a tariff is a tax on imports

scenes.narration: The phrase 'make the foreigners pay' is one of the most effective political illusions there is — because the person actually paying is standing at a checkout, not in Beijing.
That doesn't make every tariff wrong. It makes every tariff a choice — with a bill, and a very specific set of people who pay it.
scenes.caption: every tariff has a payer

scenes.narration: So the one-line truth to remember is this: a tariff is a tax on your own citizens, cleverly dressed up as a tax on foreigners.

So why are tariffs so politically popular, despite all of this? Because the benefits are visible and local — a saved factory, a ribbon-cutting — while the costs are tiny, scattered across millions of invisible receipts.
The saved factory makes the evening news. Your slightly higher prices never do.
scenes.memeBottom: your higher prices: on the receipt

scenes.narration: So the next time you hear 'and they'll pay for it,' you'll know exactly where to look for the real bill. Not on a foreign government's desk — on your own receipt.

youtube.hook: 'Put tariffs on China and China pays' is one of the most effective political illusions there is. The receipts say otherwise: a tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the domestic importer at the border, and passed on to you at the checkout. This is exactly how it works — pass-through, the hidden price hike on domestic goods too, the real winners and losers, the trade-war retaliation that makes you pay twice, and the honest case for when tariffs actually make sense. Fully cited.
